_note: Used by coach.js (fallback steps when /api/coach fails) and api/experience.js (valid track ids). fields = library tile `field` values.

student.text: Join or start a mock trial or debate team
student.why: Arguing a case out loud is the fastest way to learn how lawyers think

student.text: Ask a teacher or counselor how to shadow a lawyer for a day
student.why: Seeing the work up close tells you which kind of law fits you

student.text: Read about a landmark case argued by a woman and write 3 lines on why it mattered
student.why: It shows what the path looks like and gives you something to talk about in interviews

early.text: Sign up for the next event of your local or state bar association's women's committee
early.why: Referrals and mentors in law mostly come from people you've met in person

early.text: Volunteer for pro bono hours with a legal aid organization
early.why: It builds real experience and a record of work you can point to

early.text: Write down your three biggest wins from the last year, with outcomes
early.why: A clear record makes reviews, applications and promotions much easier

experienced.text: Offer to mentor one junior lawyer or law student this quarter
experienced.why: Your judgment is rare, and the next woman in the field gets there faster with it

experienced.text: Write or speak about one lesson from your career, on a panel or in a short article
experienced.why: It builds your name beyond your firm and gives others a map

experienced.text: Sponsor a woman for a stretch case or promotion decision
experienced.why: Sponsorship, not advice alone, is what moves careers forward

student.text: Volunteer at a hospital, clinic or health fair
student.why: Time around patients shows you what the work is really like

student.text: Ask your school counselor about a health-science program or summer program
student.why: Programs give you experience and a recommendation for later

student.text: Read the story of a woman physician and note one choice she made that you could make too
student.why: Stories make a long path feel doable

early.text: Find a mentor in your specialty through your professional society's women's group
early.why: Specialty choice and training decisions go better with someone ahead of you

early.text: Join a research, quality-improvement or community health project
early.why: It adds experience beyond clinical hours and builds your CV

early.text: Keep a one-page list of cases, projects and teaching you've done
early.why: You'll need it for every application, review and award

experienced.text: Take on a resident or student as a mentee
experienced.why: Women in medicine report that one champion changes their path

experienced.text: Teach a session or give grand rounds on something you know well
experienced.why: It builds your reputation and gives younger doctors your hard-won view

experienced.text: Nominate a colleague for an award or leadership role
experienced.why: Women are nominated less often, and your nomination counts

student.text: Build one small project (a game, a site or a bot) and put it on GitHub
student.why: A finished project teaches more than any course and shows what you can do

student.text: Join a coding club or a girls-in-tech group at school or online
student.why: You learn faster and stay longer with peers

student.text: Try a free beginner course on a topic you're curious about for one hour
student.why: Starting is the hardest part; one hour is enough to see if you like it

early.text: Contribute one fix or doc improvement to an open-source project
early.why: It's real work with your name on it, and anyone can check it

early.text: Find a senior engineer to ask three questions about your next step
early.why: Your next role depends on knowing how people made the jump

early.text: Write a short post about something you built or learned
early.why: Public work gets you noticed for roles you haven't applied for yet

experienced.text: Mentor an early-career woman engineer, or run a small learning group
experienced.why: Women leave tech at high rates, and mentors are a big reason to stay

experienced.text: Give a talk or write about a hard technical decision you made
experienced.why: It builds your standing and teaches others

experienced.text: Push for a woman on your team to lead a project
experienced.why: Visible projects are how people get promoted

student.text: Join a robotics, maker or engineering club, or start one with a friend
student.why: Building things in a team is what engineering is

student.text: Take apart or repair something and write what you learned
student.why: Curiosity about how things work is the core skill

student.text: Look up an engineering summer program or open day near you
student.why: You get hands-on experience and meet people in the field

early.text: Join your professional society (for example a women in engineering group)
early.why: Mentors and job leads come through these groups

early.text: Volunteer on a project where you can lead a piece of the design
early.why: Leading a piece shows you can own work

early.text: Document one project with photos, your role and the result
early.why: A portfolio beats a résumé line

experienced.text: Take on a junior engineer as a mentee
experienced.why: You can save them years of avoidable mistakes

experienced.text: Speak at a school or a university about your career
experienced.why: Girls who meet a real engineer are more likely to pursue it

experienced.text: Put a woman forward for a technical lead role
experienced.why: Representation in leadership changes who joins next

student.text: Enter a science fair or start a small experiment of your own
student.why: Doing real science teaches you to ask and test questions

student.text: Email a teacher or professor to ask if you can help in a lab
student.why: Many labs welcome curious beginners if you ask politely

student.text: Read the story of a woman scientist and write down the question she asked
student.why: It shows how discoveries begin with a question

early.text: Apply for a fellowship, travel grant or poster session
early.why: Small recognitions add up to a career

early.text: Ask a researcher you admire for a 20-minute chat about their path
early.why: Most scientists enjoy talking about their work, and advice here is specific

early.text: Update a one-page summary of your methods, results and skills
early.why: You'll need it for grants, jobs and collaborations

experienced.text: Mentor a graduate student or postdoc, especially a woman
experienced.why: Support at this stage keeps talented people in science

experienced.text: Review a paper or join a grant panel
experienced.why: It shapes the field and raises your visibility

experienced.text: Nominate a colleague for a prize or society role
experienced.why: Women win prizes less often partly because they're nominated less

student.text: Join an astronomy club or attend a public star-gazing night
student.why: Looking through a telescope is where many careers begin

student.text: Learn to name five constellations or planets you can see tonight
student.why: A small, doable start builds the habit

student.text: Look up a space-science summer program or competition for your age
student.why: It gives you real projects and people to learn from

early.text: Join a local astronomy society or a space-industry network
early.why: Space is a small world where introductions matter

early.text: Volunteer for a citizen-science project in astronomy
early.why: It's real data work you can list

early.text: Apply to one program or fellowship in the space sector
early.why: Even trying clarifies what they look for

experienced.text: Mentor a student interested in space
experienced.why: Your path is the example many girls never get to see

experienced.text: Give a public talk at a school or a science center
experienced.why: Public visibility inspires the next group

experienced.text: Recommend a woman for a mission, panel or leadership role
experienced.why: Opportunities in this field pass through personal networks

student.text: Start a tiny project that earns or raises a small amount (a bake sale, a service, a product)
student.why: Selling something real teaches more than a class

student.text: Ask a local business owner how they started and what they'd do differently
student.why: Practical stories beat theory

student.text: Join a business, DECA or entrepreneurship club
student.why: Teams and competitions make the learning stick

early.text: Talk to three people one step ahead of you about how they got there
early.why: Patterns across their answers show your own next move

early.text: Join a women's business or founders network in your city or online
early.why: Deals, clients and advice mostly come through relationships

early.text: Write a one-page plan with one goal and the first three steps
early.why: A written plan makes it much more likely you'll act

experienced.text: Mentor or invest in a woman founder or rising manager
experienced.why: Women-led companies often have trouble finding the first backer

experienced.text: Join or start a board, advisory group or peer circle
experienced.why: It grows your influence and your view of the market

experienced.text: Speak about a hard lesson from your career
experienced.why: Honest stories help others avoid the same mistakes

student.text: Join student government, a youth council or a model UN team
student.why: It's practice in leading and persuading a real group

student.text: Attend a city council or school board meeting and note one decision
student.why: Local government is where most students first see how decisions get made

student.text: Write to a local official about an issue you care about
student.why: It teaches you how to make an argument and get a reply

early.text: Volunteer for a campaign, advocacy group or public-interest organization
early.why: Experience on the inside beats reading about it

early.text: Find out how your local government appoints people to boards and committees
early.why: Appointed roles are often easier to get than elected ones and lead further

early.text: Write a short policy memo on one local problem
early.why: A clear memo is the best calling card in policy

experienced.text: Mentor or sponsor a woman considering public service
experienced.why: Many women only run after someone asks them directly

experienced.text: Offer testimony, a briefing or an op-ed on your area of expertise
experienced.why: It builds trust and puts you in the room

experienced.text: Join a board or commission where you can lead
experienced.why: Leadership roles train you for bigger ones

student.text: Write for your school paper, blog or newsletter, even one short piece
student.why: Published work is the fastest way to learn and the only portfolio you need now

student.text: Interview someone interesting and write up what you learned
student.why: Interviewing is the core skill of reporting

student.text: Read a great piece by a woman journalist and note what makes it work
student.why: Good writing is learned partly by taking it apart

early.text: Pitch one story to a local outlet
early.why: Editors know that unsolicited ideas are how new voices break in

early.text: Build a simple online portfolio with your 3 best pieces
early.why: It's the first thing an editor will look for

early.text: Join a professional group for women journalists or writers
early.why: Leads and mentors often come through these groups

experienced.text: Mentor a younger writer or reporter
experienced.why: One editor's belief often changes a writer's career

experienced.text: Pitch or commission a story that amplifies a woman who isn't getting coverage
experienced.why: What gets covered shapes who's remembered

experienced.text: Teach a workshop or speak on a craft lesson from your career
experienced.why: It grows your name and passes on the skill

student.text: Make something every day for a week, however small, and keep it
student.why: Habit and volume matter more than polish at the start

student.text: Show your work to one person whose opinion you trust and ask one question
student.why: Feedback is how craft grows

student.text: Look up an open mic, student show or exhibit you could take part in
student.why: A first audience is a big step

early.text: Submit your work to one open call, show or competition
early.why: Rejection is normal; the entries build your list of credits

early.text: Find an artist or performer a few steps ahead and ask how they make a living
early.why: Practical details matter as much as talent

early.text: Put your best 5 pieces in one simple portfolio page
early.why: It's what you'll send to every gallery, studio or producer

experienced.text: Mentor a young artist or offer a studio or stage visit
experienced.why: Access is often the biggest barrier

experienced.text: Curate, host or recommend a woman for a show, panel or commission
experienced.why: Opportunity in the arts passes through a few hands

experienced.text: Teach a workshop or talk about your process
experienced.why: It grows your reach and shares your craft

student.text: Tutor or help a younger student with something you're good at
student.why: Teaching is the fastest way to find out if you enjoy it

student.text: Ask a teacher you admire what they wish they'd known at the start
student.why: Good teachers tend to have specific, useful answers

student.text: Look into a teaching or education program or club at your school
student.why: It's an early look at a career that shapes many others

early.text: Observe a teacher whose classroom you admire for one lesson
early.why: One lesson teaches you more than a manual

early.text: Join a teachers' network, union or subject association
early.why: Resources, mentors and openings come through these

early.text: Document one lesson or project that worked and why
early.why: Evidence of impact helps you with reviews and new roles

experienced.text: Mentor a new teacher or student teacher
experienced.why: The first years are when most teachers quit; support keeps them

experienced.text: Share one lesson plan or method that works at a conference or online
experienced.why: It multiplies your impact beyond your classroom

experienced.text: Put your name forward for a curriculum, department-head or policy role
experienced.why: Teachers who step up shape the system

student.text: Try out for a team, or start a casual group of your own
student.why: Playing consistently builds confidence and friends who also push you

student.text: Ask a coach what they look for in a player and what to practise this month
student.why: A coach's specific tips are worth hours of guessing

student.text: Read about a woman athlete and the barrier she faced
student.why: It shows how others made their own way

early.text: Look for a coaching, officiating or club-leadership role
early.why: Leadership roles keep you in the sport in many ways

early.text: Find a mentor through a women's sports organization
early.why: Careers in sport often depend on who knows you

early.text: Track your results and goals for the season in one place
early.why: Records help you improve and help with sponsors and applications

experienced.text: Coach or mentor a young athlete, especially a girl
experienced.why: Coaching and role models are why many girls stay in sport

experienced.text: Speak at a school or club about your career
experienced.why: Visibility helps girls see it as an option

experienced.text: Advocate for a woman's team, program or resource at your club or league
experienced.why: Funding and access shape who gets to play
